narrative:
The prediction indicates a 64% chance you will leave your job, and it is this risk that stands in the way of the promotion. The strongest signal in your profile is that you have received other job offers while working here. Very few employees who stay (about one in four) ever receive such offers, so this factor weighs heavily toward the model expecting you to depart.

Your work-life balance also works against you. You described balancing your professional and personal life as difficult, a situation reported by fewer than one in ten employees who remain. This difficulty suggests that even if you were promoted, the added pressure might push you out the door.

Your experience level of six to ten years is the third most influential factor. While experience is generally positive, at this stage you are highly marketable and have likely built skills that competitors value. Among those predicted to stay, about a third share this experience range, but combined with outside offers and a stressful work-life balance, it signals mobility rather than loyalty.

What should happen next is a conversation. If the organization values you, it should address the root causes: reduce the strain on your personal time, offer a clear growth path, and ensure your compensation and recognition match the offers you are receiving. For you, consider whether a promotion here would meaningfully improve your balance and satisfaction, or whether the external opportunities you have are the better investment.
